publicationDetails.detailsText: Ang, Yuen Yuen (2025). “Polytunity: The Future of Development.” SSRN Research Note. Essay first published in The Ideas Letter (Sept 4, 2025). Open access at: https://www.theideasletter.org/essay/polytunity/

detail.abstract:
Polycrisis—a term popularized by Adam Tooze to describe the world’s interconnected crises—has become an apocalyptic buzzword of the 2020s. Yet the polycrisis appears doomed only when viewed through the lens of Western decline. For others not attached to the old order, especially in the Global South, it presents what I coin as a polytunity—a generative and global moment to rethink the intellectual foundations of modernity. 

I trace the polycrisis to its intellectual root: the industrial-colonial paradigm, inherited from past centuries of modernization. This paradigm promoted “thinking in machine mode” and one-size-fits-all templates based on idealized narratives of Western development. Applied in practice, these have produced distorting consequences across domains, from agriculture to development projects.

As a systems-level alternative, I advance AIM (Adaptive, Inclusive, Moral) Political Economy. 

Adaptive: From machine-thinking to systems-thinking: societies as forests, not toasters. 

Inclusive: From one-size-fits-all Western templates to diverse, local solutions: “use what you have.” 

Moral: From claiming neutrality to recognizing power and positionality in knowledge production.

In short, polytunity is the portal—it reframes today’s disruptions not as paralysis but as openings for systemic change. AIM is the paradigm—it provides a new foundation for studying and shaping political economies. Adaptive, Inclusive, and Moral form the three pillars of AIM—emphasizing that a paradigm fit for a disrupted, multipolar age must be adaptive in method, inclusive in scope, and reflexive in its moral orientation.

title: Understanding Gold
affiliations: TR and Duke University - Fuqua School of Business

detail.title: Understanding Gold
detail.abstract: Gold has a reputation as a safe-haven asset-useful in times of economic turmoil or inflation. However, perceptions can differ from reality. We examine the investment characteristics of gold and assess its reliability as a hedging asset. We also explore the reasons that the gold price is so high today by detailing the role of the financialization of gold as well as the push among many countries to de-dollarize. We also argue that a second demand shock that could be on the same scale as ETF introduction looms on the horizon with potential changes in Basel III regulations that would allow commercial banks to hold gold for regulatory purposes as a high-quality liquid asset. It is inconsistent that central banks hold gold as a major reserve asset-yet commercial banks cannot. Finally, using the framework of Erb and Harvey (2013), we show that based on historical analysis, when gold hits all-time highs, the subsequent multi-year returns are low or negative. This needs to be weighed against both gold hedging ability, i.e., hedging assets have low expected returns, and the possibility of increased demand from de-dollarizing countries, institutional investors and commercial banks.

title: Internet Access and Youth’s Mental Health and Well-being: Evidence from Ethiopia
affiliations: Maastricht University and Maastricht University

detail.title: Internet Access and Youth’s Mental Health and Well-being: Evidence from Ethiopia
detail.abstract: This paper offers some of the earliest evidence on the effects of internet access on adolescents’ wellbeing and mental health in a low-income country setting. Using data from Ethiopia, we document declines in subjective well-being and heightened risks of mental health disorders among young people following the diffusion of the internet. These effects are heterogeneous: adolescents from lower-wealth households experience disproportionately stronger adverse impacts, highlighting the Matthew Effect in the digital age. To address potential endogeneity, we employ multiple estimation strategies, including panel fixed effects and instrumental variable estimations. Mechanism analysis further indicates that passive internet use, particularly among socioeconomically disadvantaged youth, mediates these negative and unequal outcomes. Overall, the findings contribute to the literature on digital transformation and human capital by highlighting the complex role of social stratification in shaping the mental health consequences of internet access.

title: Seeds for Change: Global Biodiversity Narratives Contingent on Values-Based Interpretations of the Global Biodiversity Framework

detail.title: Seeds for Change: Global Biodiversity Narratives Contingent on Values-Based Interpretations of the Global Biodiversity Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) was adopted in 2022 as a global strategy to address the worsening biodiversity crisis and the widespread degradation of ecosystems. Acknowledged within the Framework is the diversity of worldviews and value perspectives on nature's roles in different societal and cultural contexts that embody the plurality of human-nature relationships. These value perspectives could influence how the GBF is interpreted and also play a critical role in how these targets are operationalised and implemented, potentially leading to diverging pathways to meet the same targets. To explore this interpretive variability, we employ the Nature Futures Framework (NFF) as a conceptual and analytical lens. The NFF offers a structured approach to capturing the diversity of positive human-nature relationships. We present a set of global narratives that were developed with a global research network of experts in various domains of conservation science. The narratives illustrate divergent visions of the future, underscoring the need for critical reflection and inclusive debate on the legitimacy of associated policy choices. In addition, we offer semi-quantitative expert-elicited estimates of change in other-non-biodiversity policy related-indirect drivers of the biodiversity crisis, together with a collection of real-world case studies indicative of alternative, value-pluralist conservation models. This conceptual reframing of the GBF as a values-contingent convention provides a foundation for both policymakers and researchers to consider nature protection policies and actions that reflect the plurality of nature values, helping to sustain public legitimacy in policy formulation and facilitating further research to address uncertainties in future trajectories for people and nature.

title: A Framework for Economic Policy Formation in Sectarian Power-Sharing Systems
affiliations: American University of Beirut

detail.title: A Framework for Economic Policy Formation in Sectarian Power-Sharing Systems
detail.abstract: Sectarian power-sharing systems present unique challenges for economic policy formation that existing theoretical frameworks inadequately address. While consociational democracy theory explains institutional arrangements in divided societies, it lacks systematic tools for analyzing how sectarian bargaining constrains economic policy choices. This paper develops a comprehensive analytical framework for understanding economic policy formation under sectarian institutional constraints, using Lebanon as the primary illustrative case. The framework integrates veto player theory with consociational analysis to explain how sectarian institutions systematically shape fiscal policy, monetary policy, and economic reform processes. Three core mechanisms emerge: sectarian resource allocation formulas that predetermine budget distributions, cross-sectarian elite coordination that blocks transparency-enhancing reforms, and informal institutional capture that overrides formal policy procedures. The framework provides policymakers and international financial institutions with analytical tools for designing economically sound policies that remain politically sustainable within sectarian constraints. Rather than ignoring sectarian realities, effective economic policy must work within these institutional parameters while gradually building capacity for broader reforms.

title: AI-Enhanced Valuation: Integrating Machine Learning Forecasts into DCF and LBO Analysis

detail.title: AI-Enhanced Valuation: Integrating Machine Learning Forecasts into DCF and LBO Analysis
detail.abstract: Traditional discounted cash flow and leveraged buyout valuation models rely on annual financial data and linear extrapolation methods, which often produce unstable forecasts and limit accuracy for companies with volatile business cycles. This study integrates machine learning forecasting techniques into established valuation frameworks using Jindal Stainless Ltd as a comprehensive case study. Our methodology employs multiple forecasting approaches including persistence models, moving averages, ARIMA, Prophet, and XGBoost algorithms applied to quarterly financial data from 2023-2025. The quarterly machine learning models, particularly Prophet, demonstrate superior stability compared to traditional annual methods, generating consistent revenue projections that eliminate negative growth scenarios common in conventional approaches. The enhanced DCF analysis yields an enterprise value of ₹33,522 crores and equity value of ₹17,463 crores, with Monte Carlo simulation providing robust confidence intervals of ₹27,716-43,950 crores at 90% confidence level. The LBO analysis reveals a 3.1x money-on-money multiple but negative 20% IRR, highlighting the distinction between equity appreciation and returns under debt constraints. Key findings indicate that quarterly machine learning forecasts provide more realistic inputs than traditional annual extrapolations, with Prophet capturing seasonal patterns missed by linear models and projecting revenue growth from ₹40,254 crores to ₹42,813 crores over 2026-2030. However, valuation outcomes remain sensitive to fundamental assumptions about discount rates and market conditions. This research demonstrates practical implementation of machine learning-enhanced valuation, showing that quarterly forecasts significantly improve stability and reliability of traditional methods while emphasizing the continued importance of human judgment for strategic assumptions and market interpretation.

title: Physics-Based Forecasts of Investment Sentiment: Evidence from Past Boom-and-Bust Periods and the Anticipated Dynamics of 2026
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Physics-Based Forecasts of Investment Sentiment: Evidence from Past Boom-and-Bust Periods and the Anticipated Dynamics of 2026
detail.abstract: This study develops physics-based forecasts of investment sentiment, drawing on evidence from past boom-and-bust periods and applying the framework to anticipated dynamics in 2026. Conventional explanations view sentiment as a reaction to news or policy events, but our findings indicate that shifts in optimism and pessimism follow predictable physical mechanisms. Specifically, the orbital geometry of the solar system alters solar emissions, which in turn influence the Earth's ionosphere and the stability of global electromagnetic standing waves. Greater stability in these standing waves is associated with higher investor optimism, while instability corresponds to increased pessimism. Using U.S. stock market data from 1935 to 2024, we test this mechanism across seven studies. An out-of-sample evaluation from 2000 to 2024 shows that orbital geometry predicts 88 percent of turning points in the S&P 500's 14-week Relative Strength Index within ±1 week (p < 0.001). These results demonstrate both historical validity and forward-looking relevance. Based on current astronomical conditions, the model anticipates that the dynamics of 2026 will resemble earlier periods of extreme dislocation, offering investors and researchers a novel framework for understanding and preparing for major sentiment shifts.

title: "Overqualified" as a Defense to Title VII Employment Protections

detail.title: "Overqualified" as a Defense to Title VII Employment Protections
detail.abstract: This Article critiques the use of "overqualification" as a defense to Title VII employment claims. Drawing on ADEA case law and the existing circuit split over whether overqualification masks age discrimination, it extends the analysis to race and sex and argues that overqualification is doctrinally incoherent, legally vulnerable, and pragmatically harmful. The Article demonstrates that overqualification often fails disparate treatment analysis because it admits that the plaintiff is highly qualified while enabling subjective employer judgments that can mask bias; it also shows that overqualification frequently produces disparate impact, since minorities and women are disproportionately likely to apply for jobs for which they are overqualified due to structural constraints including limited mobility, limited business networks, caregiving responsibilities, and wealth disparities. After diagnosing inconsistent judicial treatment and misalignment with Title VII's purpose, the Article catalogs pragmatic costs-discouraging selfimprovement and reinforcing stereotypes-and recommends that courts treat overqualification with skepticism; demand objective, job-related proof when employers rely on it; and consider regulatory or legislative clarification to prevent the doctrine from perpetuating inequality.

detail.title: Exploring Challenges and Politics of Knowledge Production in the Global South -Evidence From Bangladesh’s Aid and Development Sector

publicationDetails.detailsText: Environment and Planning C: Politics and Space, volume 43, issue 5, 2025[10.1177/23996544241299931]

detail.abstract: This article takes Bangladesh as a case study and explores the motivations (or lack of), challenges, and politics of knowledge production with a particular focus on development scholarship and practice. This piece is based on qualitative research methods and draws from 25 semi structured interviews with highly experienced and senior Bangladeshi development practitioners and academics. Empirical evidence and consequent analysis presented in this work contribute to the debates around the schism in access to resources, politics of aid, and power over knowledge production. This article also reveals local cultural contexts as consultancy works are perceived to be more financially rewarding. This is manifested through current practices that have created a condition where local researchers and practitioners feel they have no time (or incentive and motivation) to engage in knowledge production. Moreover, this article explores whether one's race and/or nationality play any role in knowledge production, and how the respondents reflect about these issues based on their lived experience. In doing so, findings of this study further the arguments of structural inequality and colour-blind approach within aid and global development landscape. This article offers a rich account of how existing practices favour staff members from the donor countries and exclude Bangladeshi researchers and practitioners from knowledge production processes. This article also brings forward an important issue which highlights that, as perceived by the respondents of this study, one's institutional affiliation with prestigious Western institutions might matter more in knowledge production (as we know it) than the content, ideas and credibility of knowledge that are generated in the global South. This article contends that by excluding, rejecting, side-lining, and subjugating knowledges produced in the global South development policies and practices will continue to manufacture a particular type of knowledge that will circumvent equity in knowledge production and perpetuate Western hegemony.

title: Application of Artificial Intelligence in the Financial System: Benefits and Challenges
affiliations: and AAB College University, Kosovo

detail.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence in the Financial System: Benefits and Challenges
detail.abstract: Rapid advances in financial technology innovations, ranging from basic accounting to artificial intelligence, have historically transformed and redefined the functioning of financial services. These innovations have increased efficiency, improved financial inclusion, facilitated customer service, enhanced decision-making accuracy, and reduced risks in financial management. Key artificial intelligence tools applicable in the financial sector, such as: automated risk assessment and credit scoring; fraud detection and cybersecurity; virtual assistants (Chatbots); algorithmic trading; financial inclusion and alternative banking solutions; as well as regulatory technology (RegTech), play a crucial role in improving financial services, expanding access to finance, and reducing risks. However, despite numerous opportunities and advantages, the use of artificial intelligence in the financial system faces several challenges and concerns. The most significant issues include data privacy protection, cybersecurity, regulatory compliance, biases, and implementation limitations, among others. This paper provides a review of the development and application of artificial intelligence, identifying the main areas where its tools are most used in the financial system. Furthermore, the paper examines the impacts of AI application, including effects on human resources, financial costs, and the regulatory framework.

title: The Clapp Theory -Dual Responsibility in Human Conflict

detail.title: The Clapp Theory -Dual Responsibility in Human Conflict
detail.abstract: Human conflict is often framed through binary narratives-victim versus aggressor, right versus wrong-obscuring the complex relational dynamics that sustain disputes. The Clapp Theory challenges this unilateral lens by positing that conflict is inherently bilateral: like a clap, it requires two hands. This framework asserts that resolution is only possible when all parties acknowledge their role in both the genesis and perpetuation of conflict. Drawing from philosophy, psychology, sociology, and case studies ranging from geopolitical tensions to interpersonal disputes, the theory explores how cognitive biases, emotional triggers, collective memory, and structural inequalities shape blame and hinder reconciliation. While recognizing asymmetries in power and harm, the Clapp Theory emphasizes relational accountability without collapsing into moral equivalence. Its applications span restorative justice, negotiation, education, and diplomacy-offering a transformative lens for conflict resolution rooted in empathy, shared responsibility, and systemic awareness.

title: Economic Vulnerability and Resilience in the Chars of Assam: A Critical Review of Poverty, Displacement and Adaptation
affiliations: Assam Don Bosco University and

detail.title: Economic Vulnerability and Resilience in the Chars of Assam: A Critical Review of Poverty, Displacement and Adaptation
detail.abstract: The paper reviews the literature on poverty, economic vulnerability and resilience in the char areas of Assam, where communities are affected by ecological fragility, institutional negligence, and widespread poverty. Based on the classical literature and new research, including theoretical as well as empirical research across the different countries in the world, the review focuses on the topics of displacement caused by riverine flood, financial inclusion, livelihood diversification, social protection, erosion and water conflicts. However, the corpus is mostly descriptive and causes are hardly inferred and there are few impact evaluations. The critical analysis of the available studies in the article points out the problem of coverage as well as identifies research gaps, also paying little attention to gender, education, and rigorous impact assessments. Although the literature together supports a multi-pillar approach to alleviating poverty, much of it falls short of providing concrete causal mechanisms. This review reveals crucial insights by unfolding the research significances of future studies and placing the chars of Assam in the global context of climate displacement, unstable livelihoods and inclusive development. However, reconceptualising study designs around causality and comparability has the potential to create actionable evidence on inclusive, climate-resilient development within one of the most vulnerable riverine landscapes of Northeast India.

title: The Effect of Credit Risk on the Financial Performance of Commercial Banks in Balkan Countries
affiliations: AAB College - Faculty of Economics and AAB College - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: The Effect of Credit Risk on the Financial Performance of Commercial Banks in Balkan Countries
detail.abstract: This study aims to examine the effect of credit risk on the profitability of financial institutions. For research, we have collected secondary data from the relevant institutions of the Western Balkan states such as Kosovo, Albania, North Macedonia, Serbia, Croatia, Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In total, there are 26 commercial banks from 2010 to 2022 that serve in these countries. We consider information from three panels that categorize state-owned banks, private banks, or multinational banks according to their ownership structure. Return on assets (ROA) or return on equity (ROE) were used as surrogates for financial performance measures, while the percentage of bad loans was used to measure credit risk (Furhmann, 2022). Where the research objective was to explore the relationship between credit risk and financial performance in commercial banks operating in the Balkan countries, to understand the factors that affect credit risk, and to suggest measures to increase the financial performance of banks in the region (Gbadamosi & Olaleke, 2019). From the evaluation results, we can see that both ROA and ROE are inversely related to credit risk (Al-Malkawi, 2019). The profitability of commercial banks in the Balkan countries from 2010 to 2022 has been shown to be related to credit risk management. As a result, financial institutions should pay more attention to credit risk management, especially bad debt prevention and investigation. Therefore, managers should pay more attention to the latest credit risk management strategies.

title: Walking the Talk? Bank Climate Commitments and Green Lending in Emerging Markets
affiliations: University of London - Royal Holloway, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and University of London, Royal Holloway College - Department of Economics

detail.title: Walking the Talk? Bank Climate Commitments and Green Lending in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: We document how banks' voluntary climate commitments predict both their green lending practices and their borrowers' environmental investments. Using structured surveys of 644 bank CEOs and heads of credit across 33 low-and middle-income countries, we develop indices of banks' green management and lending practices. These unique organizational data reveal that banks signing international climate initiatives ('talk') indeed exhibit stronger green practices ('walk') than non-signatories. We then merge our bank data with detailed surveys of 4,719 firms and show that firms borrowing from climate-committed banks are more likely to undertake green investments. Exploiting geocoded bank branch and firm locations, we further find evidence of spatial matching: environmentally-oriented firms preferentially borrow from climate-committed banks in their vicinity. These patterns are consistent with voluntary climate commitments reflecting genuine environmental orientation rather than greenwashing.

title: Religious Riders and the Sherman Act
affiliations: Duke Law School

detail.title: Religious Riders and the Sherman Act
detail.abstract:
Can corporations engage in anticompetitive behavior on the basis of religious belief? While it may seem like the answer is an obvious no, in fact this question has largely been overlooked. Instead, it has hovered at the margins of the debate over religious exemptions: proponents of religious exemptions have essentially argued that there is no harm in providing such exemptions to businesses because a competitive market will ensure consumers who might be denied services or goods by a religious firm can still obtain those goods and services elsewhere. But what if religiously minded businesses act in ways that are specifically designed to limit access to certain goods and services not just with respect to their own businesses, but others as well?

In this Article, I apply an antitrust lens to Catholic hospitals’ practice of imposing religious restrictions on secular, competitor collaborators, as well as post-sale religious restrictions on the sale of Catholic hospitals to secular buyers. Although Catholic hospital stakeholders assert that these contractual arrangements are necessary to protect the Catholic healthcare mission, I show that these arrangements are also anticompetitive. By requiring a secular firm to artificially suppress output, these agreements lead both to deadweight loss (i.e., a denial of care) and higher prices. And because there is no procompetitive justification for such market harms, these agreements violate Section 1 of the Sherman Act.

There is not, and should not be, a religious exemption to the Sherman Act. Although religious liberty is a fundamental component of our democratic system, this Article argues that there must nonetheless be market limits to free exercise.  Religious firms may enjoy a right to unilaterally refuse to provide certain goods or services on the basis of religious devotion, but they should not be permitted to enter into anticompetitive agreements that limit other market actors’ ability to fully compete in the market. Similarly, secular businesses should not be permitted to justify otherwise anticompetitive agreements on the basis of other firms’ religious beliefs.

title: Evolution of global healthcare trade networks: Structural fracture detection, topological responses, and cross-commodity dependency restructuring
affiliations: Guizhou University of Finance and Economics, Guizhou University of Finance and Economics, Guizhou University of Finance and Economics, Faculty of Natural Sciences and Mathematics, University of Maribor and Community Healthcare Center Dr. Adolf Drolc Maribor

detail.title: Evolution of global healthcare trade networks: Structural fracture detection, topological responses, and cross-commodity dependency restructuring
detail.abstract: We study the evolution of global healthcare trade networks under conditions of systemic stress. Global health crises and geopolitical disruptions have revealed the structural fragility of vaccine and medical device trade systems, yet existing research has lacked a unified framework for detecting structural fractures while capturing the dynamic reconfiguration and decoupling of interdependent networks. To address this gap, we propose an integrated analytical framework that combines graph neural network–based change-point detection, multidimensional topological metrics to trace network evolution, and a dynamic cross-network modeling strategy to examine coupling effects between vaccine and medical device trade. Using longitudinal trade data, we identify multiple critical disruptions—most prominently during the COVID-19 pandemic and the escalation of United States–China tariffs—that triggered asymmetric but significant structural transformations. We show that the vaccine trade network underwent centralized realignment and regional clustering after 2020, while maintaining institutional stability on the supply side. By contrast, the medical device trade network exhibited earlier, more episodic sensitivity to geopolitical shocks but retained a stable core architecture and greater topological resilience. Through cross-network analysis, we demonstrate a clear post-crisis decoupling trend, reflected in the functional divergence of the two systems: vaccine trade has become increasingly centralized and geopolitically managed, whereas medical device trade remains flexible and market-oriented. Our findings highlight the importance of understanding global health trade as a system of structurally distinct yet interconnected subsystems. We argue that our framework provides both methodological and empirical advances for assessing trade network resilience and can inform the design of modular, adaptive, and differentiated governance strategies to buffer future systemic shocks.

title: An Analysis of Event-Splitting Effects in Choice under Risk
affiliations: and University of Würzburg

detail.title: An Analysis of Event-Splitting Effects in Choice under Risk

declarations.ethicsApproval: IRB approval was given by the German Association for Experimental Economic Research e.V. (GfeW).

detail.abstract: We study event-splitting effects (ESEs) in choice under risk. Our theoretical model represents states of the world as intervals, allowing us to capture their spatial position within the matrix display. In line with previous research, we predict that a greater number of event-splittings increases the likelihood of ESEs. Beyond this, our model generates a novel prediction: states presented earlier in the matrix receive disproportionate weight. We test these predictions in an online experiment and find strong support. ESEs intensify as the number of event-splittings rises, though with diminishing marginal effects. Moreover, moving a sub-state to the right attenuates ESEs. Together, our results show that the frequency of event-splittings and the spatial position of states jointly shape choice under risk.

title: Legal Horizons in Smart City Innovation
affiliations: and Cravath, Swaine & Moore LLP

detail.title: Legal Horizons in Smart City Innovation
detail.abstract: Smart cities are moving from pilot to policy, forcing governments to reconcile innovation with law.  This article surveys the core legal rails needed for trustworthy urban tech: privacy and cross-border data transfers (GDPR, CCPA, PDPA; Schrems II), interoperability and open APIs (avoiding data silos and vendor lock-in), public–private IP allocation (data ownership, database rights, licensing, and procurement terms), and next-generation infrastructure built on distributed ledgers (self-sovereign identity, ZKPs, tokenized incentives, smart contracts and auditability).  It then sets out AI guardrails for municipal deployments—bias mitigation, transparency, Article 22 automated-decision rights, security against model poisoning/adversarial attacks, and the tension between explainability and vendor trade secrets (with practical tools like audit clauses and escrowed algorithms).  Across these domains, the paper offers contract strategies, governance frameworks, and standardization touchpoints cities can adopt now to integrate systems, preserve public control, and protect rights.  The throughline is simple:  when legal architecture evolves alongside technology—privacy-by-design, interoperability-by-default, equity-by-design—smart cities become not only more efficient, but also more accountable, resilient, and fair.

title: Inflation Uncertainty: Measurement, Causes, and Consequences
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University, Harvard University - Business School (HBS), Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business and University of Michigan

detail.title: Inflation Uncertainty: Measurement, Causes, and Consequences
detail.abstract: We measure and analyze inflation uncertainty in the US. We construct a novel composite indicator of inflation uncertainty (CIU) from two components: a news-based measure derived from textual analysis of newspaper articles using large language models and a market-based measure that draws on prices of options on Exchange Traded Funds and commodities. Unlike survey- or inflation-option-based measures, our index is available in real time and extends back to 1926. CIU reveals that inflation uncertainty spiked during the Great Depression, World War II, the 1970s and 1980s, following the Global Financial Crisis, and in the post-pandemic period. We highlight the driving forces behind these fluctuations in uncertainty and analyze their economic consequences. Heightened inflation uncertainty is associated with higher prices of real assets-such as gold, silver, and housing-but with lower prices of nominal assets, including government bonds, corporate bonds, and equities. Moreover, we find that increases in inflation uncertainty are followed by declines in private investment and real economic activity.

reference: De Nederlandsche Bank Working Paper No. 843
title: How do Rising Temperatures Affect Inflation Expectations?
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB) - Directorate General Research, European Central Bank (ECB), European Central Bank (ECB) and De Nederlandsche Bank

detail.title: How do Rising Temperatures Affect Inflation Expectations?

publicationDetails.detailsText: De Nederlandsche Bank Working Paper No. 843
publicationDetails.journalName: De Nederlandsche Bank Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Global temperatures are rising at an alarming pace and public awareness of climate change is increasing, yet little is known about how these developments affect consumer expectations. We address this gap by conducting a series of experiments within a large-scale, population-representative survey of euro area consumers. We randomly assign consumers to hypothetical global temperature change scenarios, after which we elicit their expectations for inflation and key macroeconomic indicators under these conditions. We find that a 0.5°C rise in global temperatures leads to a 0.65 percentage point increase in five-year-ahead inflation expectations, with effects particularly pronounced among consumers with greater awareness of climate change. Additionally, respondents expect adverse impacts of global warming on economic growth, employment, public debt, tax burdens, and their well-being. Despite these pessimistic expectations, many consumers demonstrate limited willingness to pay for mitigating further temperature increases. Instead, they place primary responsibility for climate action on governments. Our findings underscore the interplay between climate change and economic expectations, highlighting the potential implications for monetary and fiscal policy in a warming world.

title: Human Resource Management is a Prerequisite for Enhancing the Quality of Higher Education in Kosovo

detail.title: Human Resource Management is a Prerequisite for Enhancing the Quality of Higher Education in Kosovo
detail.abstract: Given its problematic past, Kosovo's economic and social development and its current resolve for a European integration process, will be a challenge that will follow for a long time. Because of the burden that state institutions carry in this mission, it is easily verifiable that the process of reform of public administration staff, both at local and central level, is failing. This is primarily because their number is too large and the government has no plans to either reduce this number or to increase their capacity and competence through educational programs of higher education. So far, the Kosovo government, specifically the Ministries of Education, Social Welfare, Labor, etc., and the local governments have no plans on how to achieve this task and the providers of higher education have not provided any program that would adequately enable employees to get re-qualified, in order to carry out their public duties more efficiently and professionally. Therefore, the requalification of staff at a higher education level is one of the essential factors that should be implemented immediately.

title: An Investigation into the Influence of Non-Performing Loans on Lending and Capital: A Case Study of Commercial Banks in Kosovo
affiliations: AAB College - Faculty of Economics, AAB College - Faculty of Economics and AAB College - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: An Investigation into the Influence of Non-Performing Loans on Lending and Capital: A Case Study of Commercial Banks in Kosovo
detail.abstract: This research is part of a series of studies that evaluate the performance of commercial banks in Kosovo, including the composition of non-performing loans within the Banking System of the Republic of Kosovo. The primary objective of this paper is to analyze the impact of nonperforming loans on the banking sector in Kosovo. The study was conducted by examining financial indicators of commercial banks, such as first-tier capital, second-tier capital, total capital, and total loans. These indicators were obtained from the Central Bank of the Republic of Kosovo, and the analysis covers a 10-year period from 2012 to 2022. Consequently, several inquiries arise: Do nonperforming loans have a detrimental effect on other financial indicators in Kosovo's banking system? What is the influence of nonperforming loans on total capital? How do nonperforming loans affect lending activities? To address these questions, we conducted a comprehensive review of empirical studies employing the SPSS model to measure the impact of bad loans. The research encompasses the period from 2012 to 2022. Upon reviewing relevant international literature, it becomes evident that numerous studies establish a direct relationship between financial indicators and non-performing loans (Çollaku and Aliu, 2021). In contrast, our study focuses on examining the impact and interdependence of non-performing loans on those financial indicators.

title: Does Climate Change Concern Lead to Greenium?
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt

detail.title: Does Climate Change Concern Lead to Greenium?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper was written as a part of my doctoral thesis

detail.abstract: To date the (non-)presence of green bond premium (i.e., greenium) has been debated. It is still unclear, however, how broadly and genuinely the notion of climate change is perceived by investors and urges them to mitigate its risk and uncertainty through green investments-a likely effective channel of greenium. To this end, I draw on the data from the US municipal bond market, which is largely populated by retail investors and segmented by states due to heterogeneous tax exemptions. I take a model-free matching approach and construct a matched bond data set to conduct a series of descriptive analyses. I find substantially higher demands for green munis in some states, which may point to the serious concern about human-induced climate change as well as to a call for environmental sustainability. Exploiting a quasi-experimental design based on natural disasters, the future agenda is to examine the degree to which an exogenous disaster-induced change in individual preferences for climate risk-as opposed to the level, which has been the focal point in extant research-leads to more demand for green bonds (relative to brown bonds).

title: Evolution and Theoretical Implications of the Utility Concept
affiliations: University of Milano - Bicocca - Department of Business and Law, Università degli Studi di Milano-Bicocca - Department of Business Administration, Finance, Management and Law and University of Milano - Bicocca - Department of Business and Law

detail.title: Evolution and Theoretical Implications of the Utility Concept

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding

detail.abstract: We review the evolution of the concept of utility in economics, addressing the conceptual and terminological fragmentation that characterises the interdisciplinary debate. This study adopts the scoping review framework to systematically analyse the main theoretical approaches, ranging from utility as preference to utility as subjective satisfaction and wellbeing. Particular attention is paid to procedural utility, i.e., the utility derived from the way decisions are made and interactions develop, divided into three areas: individual, linked to autonomy and self-determination; interpersonal, related to the quality of social relations; and institutional, referring to participation and recognition. The analysis is based on three aspects: (i) how different theoretical traditions have interpreted utility and well-being; (ii) what convergences and divergences emerge in the contemporary literature; (iii) and what implications these factors have for research and public policy. We highlight the complementarity between approaches and suggest extending economic reflection to dimensions that are central to the well-being of individuals and societies. The insights of this study have public policy implications, indicating that, through well-defined institutions, distributive justice, and welfare systems, taxpayers' hedonic utility can be transformed into the chrematistic utility of beneficiaries.

reference: The Regulation of Data Sharing in Europe: A Critical Assessment of Regulatory Frameworks, Routledge (2025), https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003248255
title: The Interplay of Data Protection, Competition Law, IP Law and Data Sharing
affiliations: University of Brescia and University of Warsaw, Faculty of Management

detail.title: The Interplay of Data Protection, Competition Law, IP Law and Data Sharing

publicationDetails.detailsText: The Regulation of Data Sharing in Europe: A Critical Assessment of Regulatory Frameworks, Routledge (2025), https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003248255

detail.abstract: The conclusive chapter of book 'Data Sharing Regulation in Europe' (Routledge 2025, eds L. Zoboli, M. Bernatt) delves into the complex relationships between data protection, competition law and IP rights, analyzing how these legal frameworks can be harmonized with pro-data sharing regulation to promote the advancement of the EU data economy. In doing so, the chapter explores the challenges and opportunities presented by these regulatory areas and proposes strategies for balancing innovation, competition and privacy while facilitating data sharing. In particular, the chapter assesses limitations imposed by IP, competition and data protection laws and names on this basis specific limitations principles which govern data-sharing. At the same time, the chapter explains how IP, competition and data protection laws may reinforce data sharing. In this respect, it names the fostering principles which govern data-sharing. On top of this, the chapter discusses the coherence of the EU data law which aims to promote data sharing, including the Data Act, the DMA, the DGA, the GDPR, the Open Data Directive and the Regulation on the Free Flow of Non-Personal Data. The chapter identifies critical gaps in the regulatory framework and proposes strategies for creating a more balanced and coherent approach to data sharing. The chapter highlights the importance of aligning regulatory frameworks to support data-driven innovation while safeguarding privacy, promoting competition and respecting IP protections. The development of Common European Data Spaces represents a promising approach to harmonizing these frameworks and addressing the challenges faced by businesses in the digital age.

title: Optimal Path for Orbital Debris
affiliations: University of Malaga and University of Malaga

detail.title: Optimal Path for Orbital Debris
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the DISE-2024 (Dynamic Integrated Space Economy) model, an integrated assessment model (IAM) designed to analyze the economics of efficient mitigation policies for orbital debris in the long-run at a global scale. The DISE-2024 model integrates an optimal neoclassical economic growth framework with a physical model of the Earth's orbital environment, capturing the dynamics of orbital debris and the likelihood of collisions. The economic component of the model determines the optimal consumption path and investments across two capital assets: Earth capital and space capital (i.e., satellites). The physical component models the endogenous generation of orbital debris, accounting for factors such as launch activity, in-orbit breakups, and collisions. The model is simulated over a 200-year horizon under various policy scenarios, including no intervention, de-orbiting policy, no breakups, reusable launch vehicles, debris-free launch systems, collision avoidance, and the European Space Agency's (ESA) zero debris policy. A key finding of the study is that mitigation policies targeting debris emissions alone have a limited impact on reducing the long-term accumulation of orbital debris. Only scenarios involving complete collision avoidance can prevent the catastrophic chain reaction predicted by Kessler syndrome.

title: Salah Bey (1771–1792): From Cobbler to Governor of the Eastern Beylik

detail.title: Salah Bey (1771–1792): From Cobbler to Governor of the Eastern Beylik
detail.abstract: This article examines the life and rule of Salah Bey of Constantine (1771-1792), one of the most prominent Ottoman governors in Algeria. Relying on both Ottoman archival sources and oral traditions, the study explores his origins, reforms in urban policy, education, and trade regulation, and the opposition that culminated in his assassination. The analysis highlights the tension between reformist governance and entrenched socio-political structures, while also assessing Salah Bey's enduring cultural legacy in Eastern Algeria through architecture, oral poetry, and collective memory.

title: Financial Covenants, Firm Financing, and Investment
affiliations: University of St. Gallen - School of Finance

detail.title: Financial Covenants, Firm Financing, and Investment
detail.abstract: This paper studies how financial covenants influence firm investment. I develop a structural model incorporating covenants and find that they allow for 4.7% higher aggregate investment relative to a no-covenants baseline. While covenants are beneficial overall, the model also reveals costs for firms attempting to avoid covenant violations. In two model applications, I find that, first, the transmission of aggregate shocks to firm financing crucially depends on firms' efforts to avoid covenant violations. Second, the model shows that earnings covenants allow for higher investment in industries with low asset pledgeability but offer no advantage when assets can be easily pledged.

title: CBDC Design in General Equilibrium: Closed-Form Adoption Thresholds and Welfare Decomposition
affiliations: Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan - S.P. Jain Institute of Management & Research (SPJIMR) and S.P Jain Institute of Management and Research

detail.title: CBDC Design in General Equilibrium: Closed-Form Adoption Thresholds and Welfare Decomposition
detail.abstract: We develop the first analytically tractable heterogeneous-agent general equilibrium model of central bank digital currency (CBDC). Households choose between cash, deposits, and CBDC based on transaction costs, liquidity services, and heterogeneous digital payment preferences, while banks transform deposits into loans subject to reserve requirements and intermediation costs. The model admits closed-form CBDC adoption thresholds and an exact welfare decomposition into three components: payment-system efficiency, distributional effects at the adoption margin, and intermediation losses from deposit substitution. We prove existence and uniqueness of equilibrium, show that the welfare decomposition tracks steady-state welfare with deviations below numerical rounding error, and provide a microfoundation for the intermediation wedge. In calibrations to ECB, BIS, and FDIC data, efficiency gains dominate under baseline parameters, making a zero spread welfare-maximizing; when intermediation frictions are stronger, the ranking reverses and high spreads or binding caps become optimal. Using spreads and caps as policy instruments, we show they act as strategic substitutes. The closed-form structure enables policymakers to map adoption elasticities and banking responses directly into welfare without relying on simulation, providing a transparent analytical benchmark for CBDC design, yielding ordinal welfare rankings and explicit policy trade-offs.

title: Balancing Equity, Efficiency, and Stability Designing Permit Trading Schemes for Sustainable Climate Cooperation
affiliations: HSE University and KU Leuven

detail.title: Balancing Equity, Efficiency, and Stability Designing Permit Trading Schemes for Sustainable Climate Cooperation
detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates how emission permit trading systems, with strategically designed initial allocations, can simultaneously balance the competing goals of economic efficiency, distributional equity, and coalition stability. We develop a novel theoretical framework that embeds participation constraints into the welfare optimization problem, ensuring countries voluntarily join a coalition. Using numerical simulation results of a RICE type of integrated assessment model, including climate-induced capital depreciation and total factor productivity growth losses, we determine welfare maximizing initial allocations of permits that address participation constraints and equity concerns. Our findings demonstrate that carefully designed permit allocations can sustain stable international cooperation while preserving climate ambitions. The welfare maximizing permit allocations exhibit a distinct temporal pattern directing permits earlier in time to vulnerable, low-income regions (notably Africa) and later to wealthier regions.

title: Environmental regulation, markup, and price: Evidence from China's paper industry
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU), Antai College of Economics and Management, Students, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management

detail.title: Environmental regulation, markup, and price: Evidence from China's paper industry
detail.abstract: We examine the impacts of environmental regulation on market power and price, with a case study of China’s water pollutant regulation in the paper industry. We find that the regulation reduces market competition thus enables surviving firms to acquire more market demand. The rising market power and therefore markup, together with increased marginal cost caused by the regulation, result in higher prices charged by surviving firms. The findings of this paper therefore highlight the importance of studying the welfare impact of environmental regulations on the consumer side.

title: A text time-series model for candidates' rhetoric during the 2020 US presidential elections: are VPs coming out of the shadows?
affiliations: Université Paris III - Sorbonne Nouvelle, France, Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique, University of California Santa Barbara and Université Paris III - Sorbonne Nouvelle, France

detail.title: A text time-series model for candidates' rhetoric during the 2020 US presidential elections: are VPs coming out of the shadows?
detail.abstract: The desire for a stable, "homogeneous people" is at the centre of the republican project of the United States (Claybourn, 2019). In a country that originally "lacked nearly all of the symbols of a real nation" (Claybourn, 2019), the sense of commonality at the base of "nationhood" is fluctuating (Claybourn, 2019). Therefore, the very definition of the notion of "people" and how it is conveyed through speeches of both the presidential candidate and the vice-presidential partner is one of the main stakes of a presidential campaign. We employ a stochastic time-series model for text data (Chalkiadakis et al., 2020) to analyse the discourse of the Republican and Democratic tickets running for the 2020 election. We aim to obtain an insight into the instrumentalisation of the notion of "people" by the two campaigns, aiming to better understand the evolution of the political landscape in the US in recent years. First, following the method of Albalat-Mascarell (2019) for rhetorical analysis, we describe the "sociocultural context" and the "generic context" of the emergence of discourse. The former is composed of the "prediscursive" components of the discursive instance (the ethos of the orator, its campaign strategy and the evolution of the race), while the latter comprises the modalities of the enunciation scene during an American political campaign. Second, we extract statistical traits from candidates' speeches to obtain a signature of the notion of "American people" per candidate. We obtain this statistical time-varying signature by focusing on the evolution, over the speeches delivered during the campaign, of discourse terms that characterise the three "modes of emergence of the people" developed by political philosopher Pierre Rosanvallon: the "social people", the "electoral people" and the "voters", and the "people principle".

title: How Do Smallholder Farmers Adapt to Water Scarcity? Evidence from the Three Gorges Dam
affiliations: Hong Kong Baptist University, Peking University and Jinan University

detail.title: How Do Smallholder Farmers Adapt to Water Scarcity? Evidence from the Three Gorges Dam
detail.abstract: We use the initial impoundment of the world's largest hydroelectric dam as a natural experiment to assess how dam-induced seasonal water scarcity was met with heterogeneous responses from households of varying endowments. In response to a persistent 12% reduction in rice yields, the wealthier households (measured by the size of farmland or bank deposits prior to the dam) compensated by increasing the labor days devoted to non-agricultural activities through out-migration, whereas the poor households increased the acreage of rice cultivation. Our study confirms that one major obstacle for farmers to choose the more effective adaptation strategy is the wealth constraint.

title: From Welfare to Desire: Social Democracy, Market Socialism, and Pathways Toward a Post-Spectacular Society

detail.title: From Welfare to Desire: Social Democracy, Market Socialism, and Pathways Toward a Post-Spectacular Society
detail.abstract:
This article explores the possibility that institutional traditions like social democracy
and market socialism can act as pathways toward certain emancipatory goals
articulated by the Situationist International (SI). While the SI explicitly rejected institutional
politics and promoted the radical transformation of everyday life in the face of
the ’society of the spectacle’ (Debord, 1967), their critique of alienated labor, commodified
urban space, and forms of mass consumption resonates with contemporary debates
on universal basic income, the reduction of the working day, participatory urbanism,
and the cooperative management of strategic resources (Weeks, 2011; Buch-Hansen
and Koch, 2018; Bauwens et al., 2019).
The article develops a conceptual framework that translates Situationist conceptssuch
as drive, dtournement, decommodification, autonomy, and spatial reappropriationinto
analytical categories that are evaluable for concrete reforms. Through empirical case
studies on the reduction of the working day in Iceland and cooperative development in
Mondragn, we examine both the conditions that enable material and cultural emancipation
and the risks of co-optation, bureaucratization, and reproduction of the spectacle
(Berg et al., 2021; Restakis, 2010).
The findings suggest that certain social democratic and market socialist reforms
can generate conditions of possibility for a post-spectacular society, fostering collective
capacity, creativity, and political participation, as long as they are articulated with
broader social movements and are designed as non-reformist reforms that challenge
the dominant logic rather than merely improving existing conditions. This approach
contributes to the literature on applied Situationist praxis and offers a methodological
framework for evaluating the transformative potential of institutional interventions in
advanced capitalist contexts.

title: Drawing the Line Between Unacceptable Audit Failure and Acceptable Audit Failure: For Building a Just Culture in a Financial Statement Audit
affiliations: Aichi University

detail.title: Drawing the Line Between Unacceptable Audit Failure and Acceptable Audit Failure: For Building a Just Culture in a Financial Statement Audit

keywords: Audit Failure in a Broad Sense
Just Culture in a Financial Statement Audit

detail.abstract:
The purpose of this paper is to examine unacceptable and acceptable audit failures and draw the line between them. This paper also suggests that drawing the line is essential to building a just culture in a financial statement audit. 

In a financial statement audit and the study of audit failure, it is critical to regard the concept of audit failure as 'audit failure in a broad sense'. This is because the auditor needs to face all audit failures, learn from them, gain valuable lessons, and prevent them in order to reduce audit failures and improve audit quality. 

However, when audit failures occur, it is unacceptable not only to punish all audit failures but also to condone them all equally. Neither accepting all failures nor unaccepting them all is just. We need to draw the line between unacceptable and acceptable audit failures to build a just culture in a financial statement audit. 

Hence, in the light of 'audit failure in a broad sense', this paper draws the line between unacceptable and acceptable audit failures. By drawing the line between them, it is possible to build a just culture in a financial statement audit. 

In conclusion, it is essential to draw the line between unacceptable and acceptable audit failures to build a just culture in a financial statement audit. This just culture is desirable not only for auditors but also for society, including stakeholders and client companies.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how coal phase-out policies can indirectly spur renewable energy growth by reshaping market demand expectation and reallocating capital. We study China's retirement of 123 gigawatts of coal capacity between 2001 and 2020 under policy thresholds. Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, we find that each coal unit retirement leads to 2.1 new solar plants and 51.3 MW of capacity in the same prefecture-year, with effects quadrupling at the province level. Firm-to-firm investment data shows that coal closures increase investment in solar firms, particularly from private investors, consistent with a forward-looking reallocation of capital. Firm-level evidence further indicates that coal closures raise solar exports and improve total factor productivity, suggesting broader industrial upgrading. These results highlight how coal phase-outs can function as an indirect green industrial policy, generating sustained market demand for renewables, stimulating private investment, and enhancing the global competitiveness of the solar industry.

detail.title: Cover Crops a Potential Water Saver
detail.abstract: This study investigates and evaluates the benefits brought by the use of cover crops in grapevine plantations and their impact on vegetative state as a result of increasing the amount of water present in the soil. Intensifying global warming phenomena has affected all ecosystems around the world, changing their specificity to new climate conditions. Due to extreme drought phenomena, the Balkan region is facing unprecedented water supply sortage, affecting both agricultural practices, including viticultural practices, and by default quality of life. The use of cover crops can become a viable choice for water resource conservation, assuring agricultural sustainability. Climate data, for 2024, analysis highlighted non-specific values for general and vine specific climate parameters. Due to extreme drought, cover crop experimental variants recorded limited vegetative growth and consequently had minimal effects on the soil water retention and vine plantation development. We aim at reestablishing experimental variants in the context of 2025 climate conditions, to obtain a positive impact regarding soil water reserves.

title: Restitution Beyond the Object: Digital and Intellectual Property Restitution with the Royal Albert Memorial Museum & Art Gallery
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Restitution Beyond the Object: Digital and Intellectual Property Restitution with the Royal Albert Memorial Museum & Art Gallery
detail.abstract: Around the world, countries are reforming national laws to enable the restitution of cultural property taken during colonial and imperial conquests. However, such restitution initiatives focus primarily on the return of physical artefacts, with less consideration for archival and catalogue records, analogue and digital reproductions, and the property or intellectual property rights associated with them. Rather than viewing these materials as separable from the physical artefact, this chapter argues they should also be included in claims to support digital and intellectual property restitution. It explores the significant potential for museums to initiate transfers using pathways already available in private law using areas of property, intellectual property, and contract law. It argues that possessors must re-examine the systems of law and practice typically applying to these materials to disentangle them to the greatest extent possible. The chapter contributes to this shift in thinking through research praxis with the Royal Albert Memorial Museum & Art Gallery in Exeter to develop pathways for digital and intellectual property restitution and, ultimately, a more expansive restitution methodology that extends beyond the physical object.

title: When Floods Swamp Banks

detail.title: When Floods Swamp Banks
detail.abstract: This article examines the impact of natural disasters, particularly floods, on systemic banking risk. The analysis is based on a quarterly panel of 61 banks located in Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan over the period 2008-2021. The results reveal a significant increase in systemic risk following floods. These results highlight the need to integrate climate risks into macroprudential frameworks, particularly in financial systems that are structurally exposed to extreme climate shocks.

title:
Green Silence: Double Machine Learning

Carbon Emissions Under Sample Selection Bias
affiliations: University of Glasgow, Adam Smith Business School, EDHEC Business School and Swiss Finance Institute - University of Geneva

detail.title:
Green Silence: Double Machine Learning

Carbon Emissions Under Sample Selection Bias
detail.abstract: Voluntary carbon disclosure collapses into a paradox of green silence: firms choose to disclose emissions based on strategic incentives (e.g., correcting vendor overestimates), while high emitters may exploit vendor estimation bias. Mirroring Heckman sample selection bias, this self-censorship skews disclosed emissions into non-random samples, distorting climate risk pricing and policy. We bridge economic problem and machine learning, proposing a Heckman-inspired three-step framework in high-dimensional settings to correct for strategic non-disclosure and ensure variable selection consistency in the presence of sample selection bias. By integrating kernel group lasso (KG-lasso) and double machine learning (DML) from neighbouring firms, i.e., using information from carbon next door, we unveil systematic underestimation: empirical analysis of 3444 unique US firms (2010-2023) rejects the null of no selection bias. Our findings indicate that voluntary disclosure induces adverse selection, where green silence rewards polluters and undermines decarbonization. Underestimation translates to a $2.6 billion shortfall in tax revenues and up to $525 billion hidden social cost of carbon. Our high-dimensional imputations also imply a substantially larger carbon premium.

title: Carbon Trading and Financial Sustainability: Intersections, Implications, and Strategies

detail.title: Carbon Trading and Financial Sustainability: Intersections, Implications, and Strategies
detail.abstract: In recent years the world has been focusing more on combating climate change and carbon trading has become a vital tool with an aim to lower the carbon emissions. The studies have shown that the financial market is essential for the success of carbon trading as they provide carbon related assets with liquidity, price discovery, and risk management. This chapter examines how carbon trading mechanisms affect the financial health of businesses and economies. It explores how emissions trading systems affect financial performance and its implications on company's profitability, liquidity and competitiveness. This study reflects how environmental regulations influence business operations, considering opportunities and challenges for achieving financial sustainability. By integrating theoretical frameworks with implication and strategies from different studies and reports, this chapter aims to inform policy makers, businesses, and investors on the role of carbon trading in promoting sustainable finance and building long-term economic resilience in the face of climate change challenges.

This paper is a response to and offers supporting analysis for Tony Atkinson's and Thomas Piketti’s claim that only rigorous Government intervention can slow the pace of the otherwise ineluctable growth in wealth inequality,which if left unchecked, is likely to have catastrophic consequences for society. The paper shows analytically, through simulation that an unequal distribution of wealth (typically the norm in industrial or post industrial society) according to the Pareto curve will, over time, lead to further massive inequalities of wealth.

detail.abstract: A spate of recent postings on social media have gotten the posting professors into hot water. These expressions are not rooted in their academic disciplines, but address public and institutional controversies: condemning Israel as a "social cancer"; condemning a faculty advisor as "racist" for the campus organization he advised. May they be sanctioned? In public institutions shelter might be sought in the first amendment. In all institutions shelter might be sought in institutional academic freedom policies rooted in national professional norms. On closer examination, however, the first amendment appears a rather weak reed to lean on; and protective policy appears enervated, the national norms in decay. This article explains how the robust, uninhibited, unfettered campus debate on public and institutional issues is now beclouded, and explores what this trend portends.

title: The Survival of U.S. Patent Damages on Appeal: An Empirical Study of Award Size and Affirmance Rates
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: The Survival of U.S. Patent Damages on Appeal: An Empirical Study of Award Size and Affirmance Rates
detail.abstract:
This study investigates the survival of large patent damages awards on appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (CAFC). Drawing on a novel database of district court jury verdicts between 2010 and 2025, the research assesses how often damages survive appellate review and whether award size affects affirmance rates. Key Findings: (1) Low overall survival: Only about one-third of damages awards survive intact on appeal once pending and settled cases are excluded. (2) Award size is decisive: Larger verdicts are disproportionately overturned, reduced, or vacated. Upheld awards average $103M, while non-upheld awards average $ 267 million. Median damages are similar (~$35–40M), showing that mega-verdicts skew the averages. (3) Cliff effect at high values: Awards above $100M are rarely upheld. Awards above $500M are never upheld. (4) Biotech vs. non-biotech: Non-biotech cases show a stronger negative correlation between award size and survival, with statistical significance. 

Implications for policymakers: The data suggest that very large damages awards, while headline-grabbing, are illusory. They rarely survive appellate scrutiny and may distort perceptions of patent enforcement. For litigants: The fragility of large verdicts may play a key role in informing the litigation and settlement strategies of patent litigants of different sizes. For the courts: The findings highlight the appellate system’s active role in overturning the majority of lower court decisions, which adds to the duration and expense of patent litigation. 

Conclusion: Patent damages awards are most vulnerable at the upper end of the spectrum. Billion-dollar verdicts consistently collapse on appeal, and damages exceeding $500M have no survival record in the modern era. The relationship between award size and appellate survival is robust, providing a better understanding of the real outcomes of patent litigation as empirical input for policy debates on patent enforcement.

title: A Comprehensive Analysis of Environmental Accounting Practices in Indian Companies: A Key Approach to Ensuring Environmental Sustainability

detail.title: A Comprehensive Analysis of Environmental Accounting Practices in Indian Companies: A Key Approach to Ensuring Environmental Sustainability
detail.abstract: As environmental sustainability becomes a global priority, businesses are increasingly integrating ecological considerations into their financial frameworks through environmental accounting, or green accounting. This study examines the reliability of measurement scales used to assess green accounting practices and provides a comprehensive review of relevant literature, policies, and standards, particularly in the Indian corporate context. Using Principal Component Analysis (PCA), the research investigates the relationships between various environmental accounting practices, highlighting the roles of financial analysis, transparent reporting, and sustainable production in promoting effective environmental management. The findings emphasize the need for corporations to improve environmental financial disclosures and invest in green production methods to meet sustainability objectives. Moreover, the study identifies gaps in current practices, suggesting areas for further research to refine these techniques and enhance corporate accountability. This analysis offers practical insights for organizations looking to integrate sustainability into their core strategies, contributing to more responsible environmental stewardship. The study also holds significance for policymakers and scholars by presenting a framework that connects financial performance with sustainability, paving the way for more informed decision-making and stronger corporate governance aligned with environmental goal

title: The Echoes of Competition in Operations: Understanding Its Impact on Consumer Review Behavior
affiliations: University of Florida - Warrington College of Business, Santa Clara University - Leavey School of Business, University of Oklahoma, University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration and Temple University - Department of Statistics, Operations, and Data Science

detail.title: The Echoes of Competition in Operations: Understanding Its Impact on Consumer Review Behavior
detail.abstract: As more businesses recognize the value of digital platforms to enhance their presence, the resulting influx of participants has led to intensified competition in the marketplace. Meanwhile, online reviews continue to be a key factor in competition, with significant implications for firms’ operational outcomes. However, the way consumers respond to competition, particularly through their reviews, remains underexplored. To illuminate this uncharted area, we investigate how the competitive environment of a business affects consumers’ tendency to write influential online reviews. We find that intensified competition, while necessitating greater decision-making effort that encourages more helpful comments, also simultaneously reduces the visibility of potential reviews and deters informative ones, leading to an inverted U-shaped relationship between competition and the likelihood of consumers posting informative reviews. Moreover, more options, due to increased competition, boost the possibility for consumers to find a match but also elevate their expectations, resulting in a similar nonmonotonic pattern between competition and the likelihood of consumers posting negative reviews. We also show that business popularity moderates the observed inverted U-shaped relationships. We further adopt an instrumental variable approach, an exogenous shock from property leasing or buying, to alleviate the endogeneity concern and conduct a survey to corroborate the underlying mechanisms. Our findings highlight the prominent role of the competitive environment in shaping consumer reviews and offer insights into platforms’ operational strategies for sustaining high-quality contributions and for businesses seeking to manage their online reputation effectively.

ניתוח אשכולות אלו טכניקות שעוסקות בארגון הנתונים בקבוצות בעלות היגיון מובחן. היגיון מסדר זה הוא אחד מאופני ההבנה והלמידה הבסיסיים במגוון רחב של תחומים כגון סיווג סימפטומים רפואיים או פילוח שוק הצרכנים. כיום, עם ההתפתחות הזמינות והידידותיות של כלים לניתוח נתונים, משתמש עם אוריינות טכנית בסיסית יכול בקלות להפעיל כלים של סיווג וניתוח אשכולות. באופן זה המשתמש לא זקוק עוד לידע אודות תהליך ומנגנוני העיבוד, אלא רק להבנה הפרשנית לגבי האופן בו יש לקרוא ולפרש את התוצאות שהתקבלו. הדבר מאוד יעיל ואמין כאשר אנחנו מפעילים טכניקות "יציבות". מנגד, הדבר מסוכן כאשר מדובר בטכניקות "לא יציבות" כדוגמת ניתוח אשכולות, שמפיקות תוצאות שונות עם כל שינוי בערכים של משתני ההפעלה. לכן, ראוי להסב את תשומת ליבו של המשתמש לרכיבים המשפיעים על החלוקה לקבוצות ועל קביעת ההיגיון המסדר. המאמר הנוכחי עומד על ליבת המשתנים המשפיעים על התהליך ומצביע על הנקודות בהן המשתמש חייב להיות בעל ידע והבנה מעמיקים, כדי שיוכל לבקר ולאמת את התוצר המתקבל.

Cluster analysis is a set of techniques that organize data into sensible groupings. The ordering logic behind such grouping represents one of the most fundamental modes of understanding and learning across various fields, such as medical symptom classification or consumer market segmentation. Today, with increased availability of AI and data analysis tools, a user with basic technical literacy can easily operate these tools with only an interpretive understanding of how to read and interpret the results obtained and no knowledge about the underlying processing. This approach is very effective and reliable when we use stable techniques that yield identical results independent of operating conditions, but is risky when we use unstable techniques, such as cluster analysis, which produce different results with each change in the values of the operating variables. Therefore, it is appropriate to draw the user's attention to the components that affect the division of data into groups and the determination of the grouping logic. This article focuses on the core factors that affect the cluster analysis process, and highlights the components of the process that require in-depth knowledge and understanding, so that users can operate these tools in a way that ensures the reliability of the results obtained.
